summary:
Russia prohibits legal gender recognition outright. The law signed by President Vladimir Putin in 2023 bans gender reassignment surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and removes the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria. Emigration has become, for many transgender Russians, the only remaining way to live openly.

Public expression is restricted by the "propaganda" statutes. The 2013 law targeted material concerning minors; it was expanded in December 2022 to cover all age groups and now reaches content that promotes "non-traditional" sexual relationships, makes minors interested in gender transition, or gives minors a "desire to change their sex". The expanded provisions explicitly reach speech that "justifies" gender transition. Enforcement has grown steeply: cases under these laws have risen eighteenfold over the past decade, more than 180 cases were brought in 2023 alone (exceeding the combined total for 2013 through 2022, with fines of roughly 26 million rubles), and fines collected under the statutes brought over 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget across two years.

The Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of the non-existent "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation governs the current risk environment. By 30 June 2025 Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in that movement or display of its alleged symbols, charges drawn from both the administrative and criminal codes. Arrests have followed the display of the rainbow flag or its colours since the designation, and between March and May 2026 nine LGBTQ organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist.

The post-designation crackdown moved quickly. Within 48 hours of the ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow; at roughly 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ life through 2025. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Foreign nationals who violate these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation. The US State Department's travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Trans people also face coercive conversion practice. A documented case describes a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour; she escaped only when police responded to a phone she had found.

Protection is sought outside Russia. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including in the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, setting the assessment standard for UK asylum claims, and Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing the country.
tangentialFactors:
The extremism designation has driven a purge and mass emigration of LGBT Russians, with reporting describing people pushed into silence, flight and self-censorship, and profiles of those caught between leaving and staying. A St Petersburg queer woman described waking up to find herself "a second-class citizen" after the ruling.

Official recognition of same-sex relationships has been foreclosed. In July 2020 voters approved a constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage, and neither marriage nor civil unions are available to same-sex couples. The European Court of Human Rights ruled in the 2021 case Fedotova and Others v. Russia that the absence of any legal recognition violated human rights; Russia left that court in 2022.

Public opinion data indicates the domestic environment a visitor would be read against: a 2022 survey found 74% of Russians said homosexuality should not be accepted by society, up from 60% in 2002, and a September 2021 survey put support for equal rights for gay men and lesbians at 33%.

Public assembly has never been permitted. Moscow authorities have never approved a gay pride rally request, and in 2010 Russia was fined by the European Court of Human Rights for systematically refusing pride parade permits.
localsOnly:
Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the state does not designate hate crimes as such: orientation or gender-identity motivation is not treated as an aggravating factor in sentencing, and hate crimes against LGBTQ people are not officially recorded.

Same-sex couples are ineligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex couples, and the 2023 legislation additionally treats as void any marriage in which a trans person marries someone of their same birth sex.

Adoption is closed to people with gender dysphoria under the 2023 legislation, and a 2024 law bars adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that permit gender transitions.

Between March and May 2026 nine LGBTQ organisations were outlawed as extremist, including the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, removing established channels for legal assistance and support.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not document how the 2023 gender-recognition ban or the propaganda provisions are applied at borders to arriving foreign nationals; the stated penalties for foreigners (arrest, up to 15 days' detention, deportation) are sourced to official travel warnings rather than to reported prosecutions of visitors.

No source in the inventory addresses airport or immigration screening for gender markers, or the treatment of passports showing an inconsistent marker.

The conversion-practice account rests on a single documented case near Novosibirsk; the scale and geographic spread of such practice against trans people in Russia is not sourced here.

Several figures (enforcement case counts, fine totals, the 101 extremism convictions, the survey percentages) are drawn from media and open-source country coverage rather than from primary court or ministry records, and are not independently corroborated in this inventory.

Whether the extremist-designation convictions could reach speech by foreign nationals published from outside Russia is unresolved on these sources.
